name: Fermented cod liver oil / butter oil (Weston A. Price)
lead: Fermented cod liver oil combined with high-vitamin butter oil is a supplement pairing associated with the Weston A. Price Foundation, a nutrition advocacy group co-founded in 1999 by Sally Fallon and Mary G. Enig to promote the research of Canadian dentist Weston A. Price (1870 to 1948).[1] Followers use it as a source of fat-soluble vitamins, aiming for well-formed teeth, jaws and facial structure, and good skin and bone development.

Cod liver oil in general is a long-established supplement containing the omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA along with vitamins A and D; it was widely used in the 1800s and 1900s against rickets.[3] Price's 1939 book Nutrition and Physical Degeneration described his travels studying traditional diets and argued that processed foods caused deficiencies and disease, with photographs of broad faces and straight teeth in groups eating traditional foods that followers still cite for facial structure.[1]

Reviewers at the time and since have disagreed about his work: a 1940 Journal of the American Medical Association review called his approach evangelistic rather than scientific, while a Canadian Medical Association Journal review praised it.[1] No clinical studies of the fermented cod liver oil and butter oil combination were found.

paras: Weston Andrew Valleau Price was a Canadian dentist, born in 1870, who graduated from the University of Michigan dental college in 1893 and practiced in Cleveland, Ohio.[1] He chaired the National Dental Association from 1914 to 1928.[1] In Nutrition and Physical Degeneration (1939) he reported on diets of communities in places including the Swiss Lötschental and among Native American, Polynesian and Aboriginal groups, claiming Western diseases such as dental decay were rare among them and that food processing removed vitamins and minerals.[1]

The Weston A. Price Foundation was co-founded in 1999 by Sally Fallon and Mary G. Enig to disseminate Price's work.[1] A separate body, the Price-Pottenger Nutrition Foundation, was established in 1952 and holds an archive of his materials.[1] The Wikipedia article on Price does not discuss butter oil or cod liver oil specifically.

Cod liver oil is made from the liver of Atlantic cod; about 20 percent of it is omega-3 fatty acids, and USDA data cited by Wikipedia list 4,080 micrograms of vitamin A and 34 micrograms of vitamin D per tablespoon.[3] Northern European folk medicine used it for rheumatism and gout, it became a bottled medicine in the 1800s, and after vitamin D deficiency was linked to rickets in 1920 it was promoted as a vitamin D source, with marketers calling it 'bottled sunshine'.[3]
Wikipedia notes that vitamin A accumulates in the liver and can reach harmful levels (hypervitaminosis A), and that one tablespoon exceeds the adult upper limit for vitamin A.[3]

In the 1920s and 1930s Price also supported the focal infection theory, which led to many tooth extractions; researchers questioned his methods by the 1930s and the theory moved to the margins of dentistry by the 1950s.[1] A 1981 critique by William T. Jarvis in Nutrition Today argued Price's work reflected a 'myth of the healthy savage' and overlooked alternative explanations such as malnutrition.[1] The Weston A. Price Foundation has published a rebuttal to critics.[1]

On looksmax.org, a thread praising Price's book argues that traditional diets produce well-developed faces and teeth across generations, while another thread revisits Price's 1930s palatal expansion case reports and discusses mechanisms for facial and systemic growth.[4][5] A T Nation thread on organ meats likewise cites Price's observations of broad faces and straight teeth among Native Americans eating ancestral diets.[6]

No studies found of fermented cod liver oil combined with high-vitamin butter oil. Related research on butter oil fractions and milk fat has looked at blood lipids and chemistry rather than dental or facial outcomes.[2] Studies of ordinary cod liver oil are covered in the separate cod liver oil article.

lore.intro: Within Weston Price-aligned diet communities and on looksmax.org, the pairing and Price's book are discussed as a route to traditional-food nutrition for teeth and facial development.[1][4][5]

claims.claim: Traditional diets rich in animal fats protect teeth and facial structure.
claims.believers: Proponents of Price's work say he found dental decay rare and well-developed jaws common in groups eating traditional foods, and attribute this to fat-soluble vitamins.[1]
claims.experts: Critics such as William T. Jarvis argued the observations overlooked alternative explanations including malnutrition, and Stephen Barrett said Price ignored life expectancy and infant mortality in the groups studied.[1]

claims.claim: Modern processed food, not genetics, underlies narrow faces and crooked teeth
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster says Price's photographs of siblings on traditional versus modern diets show the physical effect of new food products, and that populations on ancestral diets had perfect teeth and little disease.[4]
claims.experts: Critics argued Price's observations overlooked alternative explanations such as malnutrition, and Stephen Barrett said he ignored life expectancy and infant mortality.[1]

claims.claim: Price's palatal expansion cases show jaw widening can improve health and development
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread describes a 1930s case of a teenager with Down syndrome who reportedly gained cognitive, growth and breathing improvements after palatal expansion.[5]
claims.experts: A single historical case report is the basis cited; no controlled studies of these systemic claims are described in the thread or in the sources reviewed.[5]

claims.claim: Cod liver oil supplies vitamins A and D that support bone and tooth development
claims.believers: Followers describe the oils as supplying fat-soluble vitamins thought to support teeth and bones.[1]
claims.experts: Cod liver oil is a recognised source of vitamins A and D and was used against rickets, though excess vitamin A can accumulate to harmful levels.[3]

card.summary: A Weston A. Price Foundation supplement pairing of fermented cod liver oil and butter oil; no clinical studies found.
card.note: Cod liver oil is high in preformed vitamin A; the sources reviewed cover vitamin A toxicity thresholds.

quick.overview:
This is a supplement pairing promoted by followers of dentist Weston A. Price, combining fermented cod liver oil with high-vitamin butter oil as a source of fat-soluble vitamins.

Price's 1939 work on traditional diets drew both praise and criticism from reviewers, and no clinical trials of the combination were found.
quick.mechanism: Followers describe the oils as supplying vitamins A and D and related fat-soluble nutrients thought to support teeth and bone structure. Studies testing that for appearance were not found.
quick.risks: No studies of this specific pairing were found. Cod liver oil is a concentrated source of preformed vitamin A, for which the US upper intake for adults is 3,000 micrograms per day.

chain: Take fermented cod liver oil and high-vitamin butter oil
Supply vitamins A, D and related fat-soluble nutrients
Claimed: better tooth, jaw and bone development
angle.text: Followers take the pairing as a concentrated source of fat-soluble vitamins, following Price's view that traditional nutrient-dense diets produced wide dental arches, straight teeth and strong facial structure. It is also used by adults who want skin and bone support.
